stages.name: Observe
stages.instruction: Slide $Z$ (protons) and $N$ (neutrons) to build a nucleus. The chart on the right plots $(Z, N)$. The shaded green ribbon is the vallée de stabilité. Above the band the nucleus has too many neutrons ($\beta^-$ prone); below, too few ($\beta^+$ prone). Visit all three regions to advance.
stages.concept: Stable nuclei cluster along the vallée de stabilité where $N/Z \approx 1$ for light nuclei and drifts up to $N/Z \approx 1.5$ for heavy ones. Nuclei above the band emit an electron ($\beta^-$: $n \to p + e^- + \bar{\nu}$) to convert a neutron into a proton. Nuclei below the band emit a positron ($\beta^+$: $p \to n + e^+ + \nu$) to convert a proton into a neutron.

stages.name: Experiment
stages.instruction: Build each named target nucleus by setting $Z$ and $N$. Read the live classification below the chart — three canonical cases, one per stability class.
stages.concept: Same mass number $A$, different fates. $^{14}_{\phantom{0}6}\text{C}$ has too many neutrons for its $Z$: it decays $\beta^-$. $^{56}_{26}\text{Fe}$ sits at the peak of nuclear stability — nothing more tightly bound. $^{56}_{28}\text{Ni}$ has the same $A = 56$ but too few neutrons: it decays $\beta^+$.

stages.name: Evaluate
stages.instruction: The stability band, the region colours, and the classification text are hidden. Given only $(Z, N)$ on the axes, decide whether each nucleus is stable, $\beta^-$ unstable (excess neutrons), or $\beta^+$ unstable (excess protons). All four correct in one pass — a wrong answer restarts the deck.
stages.concept: Reverse mapping: given $(Z, N)$, compare $N$ to the central curve $N \approx Z\,(1 + Z/166)$. If $N$ is above the curve, the nucleus is neutron-rich ($\beta^-$). If below, proton-rich ($\beta^+$). Inside the narrow band around the curve, the nucleus is stable against $\beta$-decay.

labels.peek_tip: Compute the band centre from the geometry: for a given $Z$, the centre curve is $N \approx Z\,(1 + Z/166)$. Compare your $N$ to that number. Above by more than a few units → $\beta^-$; below → $\beta^+$; within a narrow band → stable. Do not look at colour cues — there are none in this stage.
labels.tip1: explore all three regions: above, inside, below the band
labels.tip2: same A, three fates: C-14, Fe-56, Ni-56
labels.tip3: N above curve → β⁻; N below → β⁺; inside band → stable

1.1: Slide N far above Z at some fixed Z (say Z = 20, N = 40). The dot lands above the band and turns orange — that's the β⁻ region.
1.2: Now slide N below Z. The dot drops under the band and turns purple — the β⁺ region.
1.3: For light nuclei, N ≈ Z is stable (green). For heavier nuclei (Z > 20), stable nuclei need MORE neutrons than protons — the band curves upward.

2.1: Carbon-14: Carbon means Z = 6, and the 14 is the mass number A. So N = A − Z = 14 − 6 = 8.
2.2: Iron-56 (Fe): Z = 26. The 56 is A, so N = 56 − 26 = 30. Fe-56 sits at the very peak of nuclear stability.
2.3: Nickel-56: Z = 28. A = 56, so N = 28. Note this is the SAME A as Fe-56 but with two more protons — that pushes it below the band into the β⁺ region.

3.1: First compute the centre of the band for this Z. For Z ≤ 20, the centre is roughly N ≈ Z. For heavier nuclei, N ≈ Z(1 + Z/166).
3.2: Compare N to that centre. Higher by more than a couple of units → too many neutrons → β⁻. Lower → too few neutrons → β⁺.
3.3: For Z = 6, the centre is at N ≈ 6, and the band is narrow (±2). N = 8 is above → β⁻. N = 6 is inside → stable. For Z = 55, the centre is around N ≈ 73; N = 82 is well above → β⁻.
